title: Insurers call for high earners without health cover to pay more tax
full_text:
Almost a million high-income Australians would pay thousands of dollars more in tax penalties for not having private hospital insurance under a proposal by health funds opposed to the Albanese government’s planned axing of age-based rebates for the elderly.
The number of people paying the Medicare levy surcharge – a tax penalty averaging $1500 annually for those above a certain income threshold who do not have private health insurance – has almost doubled in the past year to more than 900,000 people, new industry data shows.
Private Healthcare Australia, which represents insurers including Medibank and Bupa, has proposed doubling the tax penalty from 1.5 per cent of annual incomes currently to 3 per cent for top earners on $164,000 or more who do not have insurance.
This would mean tax hits of $5000 or more a year for top earners who decide it is cheaper to pay the penalty than fork out for increasingly expensive private health cover. The latest data reveals the number of people in that category is rising rapidly.
People earning $105,000 or more a year and families with an income of $210,000 or more must pay an annual Medicare surcharge levy if they do not have private hospital insurance. The penalty was introduced in 1997 to keep pressure off public hospitals.
There are three tiers of tax penalties for not having private hospital cover. The surcharge for tier 1 earners – people with an income between $105,000 and $123,000, or a family on $210,000 to $246,000 – would increase from 1 per cent of their earnings to 1.5 per cent.
For tier 2 and 3 earners with incomes between $123,000 and $164,000 or more – or a family on between $246,000 and $328,000 or more – the levy would increase from 1.25 to 1.5 per cent currently to 3 per cent of income, the PHA proposal to a Senate inquiry into tax rebates shows.
PHA’s modelling showed the proposal, if implemented, would increase the number of people taking private cover by 383,900 and provide the government $410 million a year in additional revenue.
This would include 157,200 people aged 30 to 49 – the age bracket the federal government hopes to encourage into private health cover by cutting the rebate for older people.
The idea is pitched as an alternative to Labor’s proposal to remove the higher age-based rebate for people over 65 to save $3 billion over four years, with the additional funding to be spent on aged care services. PHA also proposed reducing excessive private medical device prices as part of a package of reforms.
PHA said the government’s proposal would result in more than 3 million older Australians facing higher health insurance costs, including 1.32 million pensioners, which would cause up to 62,000 to drop their cover and another 200,000 to downgrade next year.
“We recognise the government is looking for savings and has to make tough
decisions, but there are better ways to achieve this than making healthcare
more expensive for millions of older Australians, particularly pensioners and people on low incomes,” said PHA chief executive Rachel David.
South Australia, NSW, Queensland and Tasmania have raised concerns that the Labor plan would drive the elderly away from private care and put more pressure on the public system.
“When Mark Butler’s own home state Labor government is telling him this policy does not add up, he has run out of people to blame,” opposition health spokeswoman Anne Ruston said on Monday.
The Australian Private Hospitals Association said in its submission that slashing the rebate would cause a couple aged 70 to pay $1614 more a year for their health cover next year and the changes would affect 3.2 million people.
Soaring health insurance premiums and a cost-of-living crisis mean more Australians are switching to cheaper policies with less cover, or dropping out of health insurance altogether. Major insurer nib said on Monday that stiff competition and activity by comparison sites were driving customer churn. Its shares fell 9.7 per cent.
This is worrying doctors, healthcare experts and private hospital operators who say the high number of “conscientious objectors” shows the current system, which is designed to punish wealthier Australians for not having the appropriate level of health insurance, is not working.
